title: The astrolabe
hookLine: Rumi: love is the astrolabe of God's mysteries (Masnavi 1.110)
carry: a love you can look through

lines: A BRASS DISK OF FINE LINES.
cards: How do you read the night sky with something that fits in your hands? In the medieval Islamic world, one answer was a brass disk covered in fine lines and tiny engraved names.
A pointer swings across the front, and a ring at the top lets it hang straight down from your thumb. It's an astrolabe.
Sighted on a star, it could help its owner tell the hour, or work out where things stood in the heavens. In Rumi's world, a learned person carried one to read the sky.
And in one line of his Masnavi, Rumi says love is exactly that kind of instrument.

teach.b: The line sits near the start of the Masnavi, after its opening song of the reed. A king falls in love with a servant girl, and she falls ill.
Doctors can't cure her, until a wise physician sees the truth: her sickness is love.

Right there, Rumi steps out of the story and says, in plain words, that the lover's ailment is unlike every other ailment, and love is the astrolabe of God's mysteries. Think about what an astrolabe does.
You don't look at it for its own sake; you look through it, at the sky. So Rumi isn't saying love is the mystery. Love is how you take a reading of it.
The next line goes on, again in paraphrase: whether love is of this world or of the other, in the end it leads us there.

A love for a person, a place, a piece of music: in his view, any of these, sighted carefully, points beyond itself. And it gathers up the week. Love called a command to act, and a little way of small things.
Wishing for others what we'd want for ourselves, and a mercy as wide as the worlds. Majnun, mad with love. Rumi hands us the instrument for all of it: a love you can look through, toward its source.

how: The Masnavi is read and recited in Sufi circles, often line by line with commentary, and its opening story of the king and the servant girl is where readers meet this line about love as an astrolabe.

o: Rumi's image of love as a tool to read God's mysteries
a map of the stars, painted on a palace ceiling
a charm worn to bring good luck in love

games.q: the line and its story — tap the pairs.
p: you look through it at the sky
in the end it leads us there

s: Rumi says love is the mystery itself
he calls love the astrolabe of God's mysteries: the instrument you read them with.
the line comes inside the Masnavi's opening story
the story of a king, a servant girl, and a sickness that turns out to be love.
Rumi says only love of God leads there
whether love is of this world or the other, in the end it leads us there.

games.q: doctors can't cure the servant girl. a wise physician examines her. what does he find?
games.why: the physician sees that her illness is love, and Rumi steps out of the story to say love is the astrolabe of God's mysteries.

practice: Choose one thing you love, a person, a song, a stretch of coastline, a dog, and look through it instead of at it, asking quietly what it is in this that you love.

Then ask again of the answer, kindness, beauty, whatever comes, and follow it back step by step without forcing an answer at the end. If you pray, you can let the trail lead into your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: The astrolabe. Rumi's picture of love in the Masnavi: an instrument you look through to read God's mysteries, not the mystery itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, from Arabic: passionate love, the word Rumi uses in this line.

carryVoice: Your line: a love you can look through. The mystery stays big; love is how you read it. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
